Armed Conflict & Security
• Poland says at least one Russian missile and a drone crossed into its territory amid one of Russia’s largest air assaults on Ukraine in months; Warsaw called it a provocation as allied military exercises took place nearby.
• Russia intensified strikes on Kyiv’s crossings and reportedly launched satellites to aid drone operations, while Ukraine’s earlier hit on the Crimean Bridge sharpened tensions.
• The White House replaced its top cyber-security official after a series of major online outages, as experts warned of growing AI-linked threat vectors; separately, the FCC approved a rule allowing prisons to jam contraband cellphone signals.
• Turkey began receiving jet-powered Kizilelma drones capable of air-to-air combat, and Iraq deployed federal forces to Jurf al-Sakhar after a deal with an Iran-backed group, underscoring shifting military capabilities and alignments.
Why it matters: Escalation around Ukraine’s war risks NATO spillover, while technological and policy shifts—from cyber defenses and signal jamming to advanced drones—are rapidly reshaping the security landscape.

Society & Human Rights
• South Africa reported nearly 600 women killed in three months, prompting calls for stronger measures against gender-based violence.
• Nigeria advanced plans to end jail terms for attempted suicide, aligning with mental health advocacy and legislative reform efforts.
• South Korea caught 111 students using banned devices in the high-stakes Suneung exam, highlighting tighter anti-cheating measures.
• A US judge rebuked ICE for “making a mockery” of court orders with an instant re-arrest policy, finding officials in contempt before the practice was halted.
• The owner of Pontins was fined £1m after a fatal 2019 ceiling collapse at a Somerset holiday park.
Why it matters: From legal reforms to accountability for state and corporate actors, these developments reflect intensifying scrutiny of public safety, justice, and rights protections.

Climate & Environment
• Climate talks in Turkey were roiled as fossil-fuel language was removed from draft text and African ministers demanded delivery of existing finance pledges; civil society branded Cop31 among the “worst ever.”
• The IEA warned data center electricity use could double by 2030 as AI adoption grows, intensifying pressure on grids and climate goals.
• Extreme weather and hazards persisted: a tropical cyclone opened the Southwest Pacific season, the UK braced for the coldest night of autumn, and California faced the biggest waves in years.
• The US held its first deep-sea mining lease sale near American Samoa despite a court voiding the environmental clearance, prompting local outcry.
Why it matters: With talks deadlocked over fossil fuels and finance as climate impacts and energy demand accelerate, political will and policy clarity remain pivotal to credible action.

• The UK and EU agreed a “reset” deal to ease trade checks, link emissions systems and start a youth mobility scheme, though tuition fee levels for EU students remain unresolved.
• European leaders signaled readiness for talks with Russia on Ukraine under a united negotiating position, even as battlefield dynamics remain volatile.
• Myanmar and China objected to the ICJ’s landmark ruling on Rohingya genocide, underscoring fraught accountability and diplomatic tensions.
• Trump, Putin and Xi pledged to boost global petrol supplies, though analysts questioned feasibility amid wars and market constraints.
• Major powers look set to block UN negotiations on banning lethal autonomous weapons, despite support from over 70 countries.
Why it matters: Amid shifting alliances and contested rulemaking, Europe seeks pragmatic resets while global powers test norms on energy, accountability and emerging military technologies.

• Sanofi lined up a large takeover target to address its sector-low valuation, signaling renewed big-ticket pharma M&A.

• Researchers documented a woman’s decades-long hibernation-like state, renewing interest in human metabolic downregulation.
Why it matters: Unraveling how neural housekeeping and immune signaling change with age could yield therapies to slow cognitive and systemic decline.

• Space science milestones: BepiColombo began entering Mercury orbit, and Europa’s persistent sodium cloud points to an oceanic origin.

• Research updates ranged from ancient giant orcas likely preying on whales to high-altitude protection for bees against mites and a new model to predict superconductors’ critical temperatures.
• SpaceX lenders reportedly want valuable chip collateral kept on Earth even as Starfactory output ramps, reflecting investor caution in fast-scaling space ventures.
Why it matters: Reliability and resilience—from digital infrastructure to biological and space systems—are under scrutiny as complexity and ambitions grow.

Why it matters: As powerful agents move from labs to devices, tensions between capability, privacy, safety and infrastructure are shaping AI’s path to mainstream use.

Climate & Environment.title: California’s coastal communities on alert as biggest waves in years hit state
Climate & Environment.text: Hazard warnings issued throughout week after powerful swells and waves of more than 9 metres recordedMultiple coastal hazard warnings were issued this week across California as successive areas of low pressure generated powerful swells and large breaking waves for coastal communities. Beaches and piers were closed last weekend as large waves crashed into California’s coastline. Offshore National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration buoys recorded wave heights of greater than 30ft (9 metres) last Friday. The Monterey, California, buoy recorded a wave height of 34.1ft, which would make it the highest reading in 30 years.Coastal warnings extended from last weekend through this week, with alerts extending until Friday night. Waves of 10-18ft are expected, with local sets of 18-22ft for San Luis Obispo county beaches and Santa Barbara county central coast beaches. These Pacific storm systems are also bringing unsettled conditions across the western US, with heavy rain, mountain snow, and strong winds through the coming days. News reports claimed that the strike killed more than 175 people, most of them children. The U.S. president and military denied responsibility. In the age of generative AI and all things deepfake, everyone—including me—was skeptical of the video’s authenticity.I get this type of request a lot. For the past three decades, I’ve been developing mathematical and computational techniques to analyze and detect manipulation in digital media. Over this time, I think it’s fair to say that I, like most people, have approached visual recordings with a “presumption of authenticity”: If a skeptic claims that a recording is fake, the burden of proof is on them.In today’s world of generative AI, however, I think we need to shift this stance to a “presumption of fake.” That is, the burden is now on the creator to prove that their content is real. While this new stance may seem unfair to legitimate creators, I think it both reflects reality and points to a future where we will once again be able to trust that most online media is what it appears to be.The forensic approach to deepfake detectionEven last March, I was already tilting toward a presumption of fake. My initial response to the reporters was something along the lines of, “I am suspicious of the video because the quality is low, it emerged weeks after the bombing, and it is only being distributed by an Iranian news agency with a less than stellar record of accurate reporting.” Given the potential implications if the video was indeed real, however, I resigned myself to spending my Saturday morning analyzing it.I first reasoned that if the Tomahawk missile was digitally added to each frame of the video without taking into consideration the camera motion, we might see a physically implausible missile path. So I aligned the video frames using a stationary background landmark as a reference. In the updated video, the missile did, in fact, move in a nearly linear trajectory. (See the yellow dots in the composite shown below.) I next asked if the size (in pixels) of the missile in the video was plausible. Under some reasonable assumptions, I estimated that the missile in the video corresponded to a 6-meter Tomahawk at a distance of approximately 100 meters. The distance seemed plausible from the scene and was also consistent with the delay of 0.3 seconds from visible impact to the sound of impact, given that sound travels at 343 meters per second.  Composite photo composed of frames from a video of the Tomahawk strike reveal’s the missile’s trajectory.Hany Farid; Source: Mehr NewsDespite the mounting evidence, though, I struggled to refine my answer for the reporters. My skepticism was fueled by a recent study I worked on with colleagues at the University of California, Berkeley, that showed how hard it is to distinguish real from fake videos. Observers are now so suspicious of videos in general that they have trouble convincing themselves that a video is real. But after a few more hours and a few more analyses with the missile video, I finally decided that it was authentic, and I gave the reporters my updated view.This analysis marked a turning point for me. I realized I was just like the participants in our study: The lack of artifacts was not enough to readily convince me a video is real. I had flipped from a presumption of real to a presumption of fake.Signaling a video’s provenanceWhen the visual record is no longer reliable, what can we do? The types of forensic analyses that I routinely perform do not currently operate at internet scale and speed. But provenance signals can. These signals include content credentials and watermarks that are inserted or embedded at the time of creation or recording. Credentials that follow the C2PA standard, for example, attach a cryptographically signed manifest to a photo or video at the moment of capture; this metadata records the device, the time and location of the recording, and any subsequent edits. Because the manifest is signed, any tampering with either the content or its history can be detected later by machine. Watermarks, like Google’s SynthID, embed an imperceptible signal directly into the pixels or audio samples that identifies the content’s origin. Apple recently took these ideas a step further. On some of its newest iPhones, the camera sensor can cryptographically sign the raw pixel data as it’s captured. That signed data is then developed into a reference image saved alongside the normal, editable photo. Anyone can then compare the two and see exactly what, if anything, was changed.These provenance signals are often criticized as being only a partial solution or vulnerable to attack. This is true if we think of them as mechanisms for catching bad actors. But that’s not what they’re supposed to do. Their purpose is to let good actors prove that their audiovisual recording is what it claims to be.Provenance signals thus need not be adversary-proof. Instead, these signals are part of a new reality in which consumers, journalists, and the courts must adapt to a presumption of fakeness. If enough good actors adopt these mechanisms, they can begin to drown out bad actors. In other words, we have to switch from a model of “catch the bad actors” to “empower the good actors.” Real-time verificationThis switch from trust to distrust of digital media has expanded to include routine video calls.In September 2024, for example, Senator Ben Cardin (D-Md.), then chair of the Foreign Relations Committee, received a video meeting request from Dmytro Kuleba, who until a few weeks earlier had been Ukraine’s foreign minister. During the call, Cardin became suspicious when, out of character, Kuleba pressed him on whether the U.S. should allow Ukraine to fire long-range missiles into Russia. Cardin ended the call. Later, the State Department confirmed that Kuleba had never requested the meeting, and the Senate security office warned staff that foreign adversaries, possibly Russian, would likely try similar faked meetings again.All it takes to conduct this type of impersonation is a face-swap or avatar deepfake, along with voice conversion, both of which substitute the speaker’s face and voice for deepfaked versions in real time. These technologies are readily available in commercial products and open-source libraries and run on nothing more powerful than a modern laptop.This video illustrates the current state of face-swap deepfakes.Farid’s Company GetReal Shows How Real Deepfake Videos Look Today  Your browser does not support the video tag. Provenance firms have to move fast to detect real-time deepfakes. Hany Farid, GetRealUnlike the Tomahawk video, which I could sit with for a morning analyzing frame by frame, a live video call offers no time for human analysis. On the other hand, real-time deepfakes pose new challenges for their creators: A fake video call has to be generated at around 24 frames per second to fool the eye into perceiving realistic motion. As a result, the deepfake video call software has to take shortcuts, such as simplifying faces and how they interact with their surroundings, and allowing some drift between audio and video or between video frames. The human eye doesn’t notice the shortcuts, but we can forensically expose them.Provenance signals should eventually play a role here. Video calling software could apply the same cryptographic signing to each frame of a live video stream that Apple now applies to still photographs. A face-swap necessarily occurs between a speaker’s camera and the video-conferencing software, and so the software could verify in real time whether the frames it’s receiving were signed by a physical camera sensor or whether they were altered in transit. As before, the burden shifts from catching the impersonator to allowing real participants to prove they are who they claim to be. For the first two decades of the digital revolution, forensic analysis—finding the telltale traces of manipulation—was enough to adjudicate most questions of authenticity. The AI revolution, however, has changed the scale and speed of manipulation beyond what forensics alone can handle. To believe a recording is real now, it must also carry a provenance signal from the point of recording. The two approaches work together, with provenance allowing good actors to be trusted, while forensic analyses root out the bad actors.

Artificial Intelligence.title: Community-Focused Academic Brings AI Tools to Colorado Farmers
Artificial Intelligence.text: Many farmers and ranchers in eastern Colorado are curious about artificial intelligence, but they don’t have a local tech-savvy person to show them how to use it. Xue “Alice” Dong has made that her job.Dong, an IEEE senior member, is an extension regional specialist with the Colorado State University Extension, CSU’s outreach arm. She works in Logan County and serves a 10-county farming area in Colorado’s northeast corner. Her job is to turn university research into practical help for the people who live there.Xue “Alice” DongEmployer Colorado State University Extension in Logan CountyTitle Extension regional specialistMember grade Senior memberAlma maters Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot; Beijing Normal University; State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse; Colorado State University GlobalShe built the AI-Powered Agritourism Chatbot (AgriTourismAI.com), which helps farmers and ranchers launch and run “agritourism” businesses. Agritourism is when farmers open their property to visitors for fun, education, or shopping events. Familiar examples include pick-your-own fruit orchards, lessons on how to grow vegetables, and sales of handmade products.Dong also teaches workshops where she shows farmers and ranchers how they can use AI tools to help grow and manage their business.She says she sees herself as a link between the university and the countryside.“We [extension specialists] act as a bridge,” she says. “We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”Many farmers and ranchers are older, and they typically have no technical training. Often their children and grandchildren have left the farm to work in a city or otherwise aren’t around to teach them about new tools. Without help, the benefits of AI could pass the farmers by. Dong’s workshops give them a way in.Dong was named a finalist in the 2026 GenAI for Good Challenge for her AgriPivot AI Agent. The challenge was organized by IEEE Humanitarian Technologies and theU.N.’s International Telecommunication Union, and her project was selected from 318 teams across 79 countries. She also won the 2026 Award for Innovation from the National Extension Technology Community (NETC), and both the 2025 national and Western regional Educational Technology Awards from the National Association of Community Development Extension Professionals (NACDEP).She has secured seven competitive grants totaling more than US $250,000 as principal investigator or co-principal investigator, including funding supported by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture.An early love of design and problem-solvingDong was born in Beijing. Both her parents are doctors.As a child, she liked drawing new and inventive things. Sketching, she says, lets her picture solutions to problems in her head and put them on paper as practical designs.That habit grew into a way of relating to her surroundings.“I’ve always had a passion to create something tangible that can solve problems in the real world,” she says.She doesn’t credit a single mentor for the direction her life has taken. Instead, she says all her teachers helped lay the groundwork for her career.She attended the Inner Mongolia Normal University, in Hohhot, an institution that trains teachers. She earned two bachelor’s degrees there in 2013—one in geographical science and one in education.She then earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction from Beijing Normal University in 2016.That year, she moved to the United States to continue her graduate studies at the State University of New York College of Environmental Science and Forestry, in Syracuse. She earned a master’s degree in environmental biology in 2020.From outreach to extension workAfter earning her second master’s degree, she joined Paul Smith’s College, in Paul Smiths, N.Y., as an education and outreach coordinator.She managed several national watershed projects to protect rivers, lakes, and aquifers. Watersheds are areas of land from which water drains into bodies of water.She also undertook invasive-species-prevention projects, wrote grants to secure project funding, and designed two educational websites and several outreach publications. One website, Maintain the Chain, helps lake residents, boaters, and visitors from around the world keep invasive species out of the Fulton Chain of Lakes in New York’s Adirondack Park.In 2022, she joined Stewards of the Coast and Redwoods as program manager. The nonprofit, based in Guerneville, Calif., works with California State Parks to protect, restore, and educate the public about the parks along Sonoma County’s coast and the Russian River area. The region is known for its redwood forests, wineries, and resort towns.She left in 2023 to join the CSU Extension as a regional specialist, a title she still holds.Her employer is part of the Cooperative Extension System, a nationwide network run by land-grant universities, schools founded with federal grants to teach farming and other practical subjects. Extension faculty and staff share what researchers at their universities learn with the citizens of those states.The cooperative system operates on three levels. It is overseen federally by the Department of Agriculture’s National Institute of Food and Agriculture, managed statewide through land-grant universities, and delivered locally by county offices and Extension agents across more than 3,000 counties.The work goes well beyond farming, Dong says, also covering community and economic development, health initiatives, and the 4-H program, which teaches children hands-on skills in agriculture, science, leadership, and citizenship.Extension faculty members’ performance is judged on their research, teaching, and service to the community, Dong says—similar to the way professors in academia are evaluated. The difference, she says, is the audience: Professors teach students; most extension specialists teach adults, including farmers, ranchers, and community leaders. The setting is different, too. Dong doesn’t commute from the campus to the countryside; she lives and works in it. Her office is in Sterling, a small rural town. But her projects serve the whole state, and many of the people she helps live one to four hours’ drive away. So, most of her work with farmers and ranchers happens by email, phone, and virtual meetings. County fairs, farmers markets, and agricultural events give her chances to meet large groups of them in person.She can’t just hand Colorado residents research findings and expect them to figure out the information they need, she says.“We need to translate that research into something more practical, and easier to use, that farmers and ranchers can understand immediately,” she says.Dong also focuses not on only on whether people use AI, but also on how they use it. In 2026, she and Paul Hill from Utah State University Extension published “From Access to Governance: Generative AI Literacy for Extension Professionals and Small Businesses, and a Governance-Aware Design Framework” in the journal AI. The paper offers a framework for helping Extension professionals and small businesses adopt generative AI responsibly.How her AI chatbot helps farmers and ranchersIn 2025, Dong earned a third master’s degree, in artificial intelligence and machine learning, from CSU Global.She immediately put those skills to work on agritourism, she says. She built the chatbot in Python, a popular programming language. It answers typed questions, and its user interface looks much like ChatGPT’s, but it works differently. Under the hood, it uses retrieval-augmented generation, a technique that has the AI look up information in a set of trusted documents before it answers. Dong curated that collection from Extension publications, so the chatbot’s answers rest on authoritative sources and are less likely to be made up. She presented the project at NeurIPS 2025 (Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems). The code is openly available on GitHub, so other Extension offices can adapt it.The bot runs in a web browser rather than as a phone app. Many farmers she works with don’t own a smartphone, Dong says, but nearly all have a computer, tablet, or other gadget that can connect to a website. The bot works on any of them, with no app to download.Extension specialists “act as a bridge. We bridge our campus to the rural communities we serve.”Farmers often ask the bot how to attract visitors and how to write a business plan. A farmer thinking about opening a corn maze, for example, can ask how to price admission, what kind of insurance to carry, and which permits to get. The bot also gives advice on managing risk.One of her test sites was Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch, in eastern Colorado. Dong documented how the ranch put AI to work in a peer-reviewed case study, “Revolutionizing Agritourism with AI and Machine Learning: A Case Study of Prairie Ridge Buffalo Ranch in Colorado,” published in 2025 in CABI Tourism Cases.Surveys and interviews she conducted with other users showed that people find it’s easy to use the bot, learn from it, and act on its advice, she says. She is preparing the full results for publication.Her work extends beyond agritourism. In 2026, she contributed an AI assistant to Project Pythia, an open-science program funded by the U.S. National Science Foundation and led by the National Center for Atmospheric Research (NCAR). The AI assistant turns raw airport weather report data into plain-language guidance for farmers and other non-technical users, and it tells users when data is missing rather than guessing.She also teaches workshops on AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini. She has taught her workshop 20 times to more than 200 entrepreneurs and business owners, who came from 32 Colorado counties. In follow-up surveys, 90 percent of participants reported trying at least one new AI task in their business. Some of the workshops take place at a community center run by the Logan County Economic Development Corp., in Sterling. She has also co-hosted the workshops with the Rural Community Assistance Corp., Colorado Startup Week, and Boulder Startup Week. And she occasionally presents them as webinars, so people don’t have to travel.Her outreach has taught her that many farmers are eager to try new tools, she says. She shows them how simple her chatbot is to use.She also offers advice to high school students drawn to the field. Extension specialists each have a specialty, such as livestock, natural resources, food systems, or 4-H. Students should pick one based on their passion, she says.Land-grant universities offer related programs at the bachelor’s and master’s levels. For graduate students, she adds, Extension offers a third career path beyond academia and industry: “You apply advanced skills directly to the communities that need them.”How IEEE membership supports her careerDong joined IEEE in 2025 and soon was elevated to senior member. Her professional home is the IEEE Society on Social Implications of Technology. She also serves as vice treasurer of the IEEE Denver Section’s Young Professionals group.IEEE supports all three parts of her job, she says. For research, she presented “Entrepreneur AI Agent: Empowering Small Businesses and Bridging the Digital Divide through Context-Aware Generative AI” at the 2026 IEEE Global Humanitarian Technology Conference (GHTC). For teaching, she has offered to bring her AI workshop to Denver Section members and local entrepreneurs. For service, she reviews papers for IEEE conferences.IEEE conferences matter most to her, she says: “Through them, I can present my research and network with other researchers in the field.”She attended the IEEE World Forum on Public Safety Technology in Boulder, Colo., in September 2026. The event, she says, opened her eyes to many new projects underway across IEEE.Still, she says, her work always points back to the farms and ranches of eastern Colorado. Its people are curious, she says, but they can’t make the leap to new technology alone.“They really need this kind of a bridge,” she says.

Entertainment.title: Licensed to Dress: Will Jonathan Anderson's Dior Re-Tailor James Bond?
Entertainment.text: When Amazon MGM officially tapped Robert Pattinson as the next James Bond, it didn't just shake up British cinema—it ignited a massive high-fashion turf war. While the battle for 007's wrist dominates watch forums, the battle for his wardrobe is equally fiercely contested.Since Quantum of Solace in 2008, Tom Ford has served as the official tailor to MI6, outfitting Daniel Craig in razor-sharp, ultra-fitted suits that defined the era. However, Pattinson enters the franchise with a massive LVMH trump card: he has been a marquee global ambassador for Dior since 2013. Now, with the visionary Jonathan Anderson at the helm as Creative Director in this new era (2025 and beyond), the stars have aligned for a radical, hyper-stylish overhaul of the cinematic super-spy.Anderson is famous for blending traditional heritage tailoring with experimental volumes, technical pragmatism, and a touch of playful, subversive irreverence. If Pattinson brings his Dior contract into the 007 universe, it would mark a seismic shift from Tom Ford’s rigid traditionalism to Anderson’s avant-garde elegance.By pulling straight from Jonathan Anderson's Dior Men vision and Pattinson's own real-world Dior moments, here are five quintessential James Bond archetypes that would redefine the cinematic super-spy:The High-Stakes Meeting: The Sleek Tailored SuitThe Look: No Bond wardrobe is complete without a striking, perfectly tailored suit for a high-stakes meeting in a sun-drenched, exotic locale. Here, Pattinson brings an effortless 007 presence to a sleek, classic grey Dior suit. Whether it’s a sharp single-breasted silhouette with a crisp collar and tie, a commanding white double-breasted variation, or an intense all-black ensemble featuring a matching suit, shirt, and tie, Anderson's Dior blends traditional elegance with a modern sensibility. It can also easily be pared down with a blue shirt underneath to adapt to less formal situations. Ultimately, it is the perfect armor for stepping off a speedboat to confront a billionaire villain on their private island. The Avant-Garde Gala: The Subverted TuxedoThe Look: Bond is famous for his black-tie casino scenes, but Jonathan Anderson’s Dior brings a brilliantly subversive edge to eveningwear. Here, Pattinson proves that 007's formal attire doesn't have to be a rigid, traditional tuxedo. Featuring a cropped, double-breasted jacket and a dramatic, sweeping white scarf in place of a standard bow tie, this look is bold, artistic, and completely unexpected. It is the ultimate ensemble for infiltrating an exclusive avant-garde art auction or a high-society gala where blending in means pushing the boundaries of high fashion.The Headquarters Debrief: Elevated KnitwearThe Look: When 007 is back in London receiving his mission from M, the wardrobe shifts to sharp, office-ready sophistication. Instead of a rigid three-piece suit, Jonathan Anderson’s Dior offers a modern, intellectual approach to spycraft. This layered runway look features a beautifully textured grey V-neck sweater layered over a crisp light blue shirt and a distinctively knotted tie. It’s a refined, smart-casual ensemble that proves Bond can command a room at MI6 headquarters just as effortlessly as he can on the battlefield.The Urban Evasion: The Voluminous TrenchThe Look: The trench coat is a non-negotiable staple for any cinematic spy, but Jonathan Anderson elevates it from a functional raincoat to a piece of dramatic, high-fashion outerwear. This sweeping olive green Dior trench, featuring an oversized, belted silhouette and a contrasting brown collar, provides incredible cinematic movement. Paired with tactical boots and loose trousers, it is the ultimate undercover armor for Pattinson’s Bond as he trails a rogue operative through the rainy, neon-lit streets of Berlin or Tokyo.The Eccentric Lair: The Subversive Tailored JacketThe Look: When the mission takes Bond to an eccentric tech-billionaire villain's private island retreat, standard eveningwear simply won't blend in. Jonathan Anderson is a master of subverting traditional menswear, perfectly illustrated by this avant-garde upper silhouette of the modern Bar Jacket. Highlighting a sharply tailored, textured blazer with bold formal black lapels layered over a crisp, high-neck white collar, this look is pure high-fashion disruption. The beautifully structured jacket allows Pattinson’s 007 to seamlessly infiltrate the ranks of the hyper-wealthy elite, providing him with a sophisticated yet undeniably eccentric armor for a high-stakes showdown.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: Vintage Modern Reimagines Classic Muscle With the 840-HP Vintage Fastback
Entertainment.text: SummaryVintage Modern debuts the bespoke Vintage Fastback, pairing a handcrafted carbon-fiber body with a modern S650 chassis.Featuring a 486-horsepower V8, with an optional Whipple supercharger boosting output to 840 horsepower.Commissioned to order, pricing starts at $295,500 USD.Atlanta-based luxury vehicle builder Vintage Modern has unveiled a new addition to its range with the all-new Vintage Fastback. Unveiled at the inaugural American edition of Retromobile New York, the vehicle introduces a bespoke, classic-inspired silhouette engineered atop a contemporary 2026-27 S650 platform.Rather than restoring an old chassis, Vintage Modern handcrafts each Fastback from the ground up using modern underpinnings. Over 900 hours of craftsmanship go into each vehicle, pairing carbon-fiber body panels with billet-aluminum accents across the grille, door handles, and mirrors. A long hood with a functional scoop, sculpted side intakes, and full-width taillights give the coupe a wide, aggressive stance. Inside the cabin, it’s thoroughly modern, featuring digital screen, leather upholstery, and three distinct seat stitching patterns alongside an optional JL Audio sound system.Under the hood lies a 5.0-liter V8, delivering 486 horsepower and 418 pound-feet of torque. Drivers seeking an even higher output can opt for a 3.0-liter Whipple supercharger that pushes performance to 840 horsepower and 615 pound-feet of torque on 93-octane fuel. The engine is mated to either a six-speed manual transmission with rev matching, or a 10-speed paddle-shifted automatic. Additional notable features include a MagneRide adaptive suspension system, Brembo brakes, and a four-mode active exhaust. Unlike traditional restomods, the Fastback is built to meet Federal Motor Vehicle Safety Standards and includes eight airbags, crumple zones, and electronic stability control.Currently on display at Retromobile New York through November 22, each Vintage Fastback is commissioned to order in over 40 standard paint finishes or bespoke paint-to-sample options. Pricing starts at $295,500 USD, with allocations available now through Vintage Modern’s website.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Entertainment.title: beabadoobee Shares Long-Teased Fan Favorite “No Punctuation” From Upcoming Album
Entertainment.text: Summarybeabadoobee announced her fifth studio album, Bananas 4 Cats, arriving February 19, 2027.Lead single “No Punctuation” trades Pylon's rock edges for an intimate, breezy acoustic sound recorded in east London.Following a surprise live debut at London's O2 Arena, the track centers on themes of home and devotion.beabadoobee has announced Bananas 4 Cats, her fifth studio album, on the same day as the release of its first single, “No Punctuation.”The news comes less than two months after the release of her Pylon album, which reached the Top 10 on the Billboard 200 and became her second consecutive UK number 1. It also follows her first US and UK arena tours, which wrapped with sold-out shows at Madison Square Garden, The Kia Forum and London’s O2 Arena.Bea frames the two records as different sides of the same person. Pylon was written and recorded on the road with a large cast of collaborators, while Bananas 4 Cats centres on the idea of home: it was made in her East London living room with only a friend, her partner and her cats for company. “I just needed to write an album like this after Pylon,” she says. “It happened naturally, I got back home and felt inspired, and made another album.”“No Punctuation” has near-mythical status among fans, who have traded snippets of it for more than four years. It only joined the setlist of "The Powerlines Tour" this week, and the O2 show ended with meowing over the sound system as the lights came up, a hint of what was coming. The finished song leans fully into Bea’s softer side. Acoustic guitar strums at an unhurried mid-tempo while reversed synth loops and light percussion gather behind it, and the lo-fi textures thicken until the track settles into a looping, hypnotic outro. True to the title, her vocal lines run into one another without hard stops, so the song feels like one unbroken thought.Lyrically, it’s a devoted love song about finding home in another person. The narrator has no wish to be anywhere else, because the person beside her already feels like home, and the chorus boils that feeling down to a simple, repeated declaration that this person is everything. After Pylon’s rougher, louder edges, it’s a tender first look at an album built around comfort and closeness.Listen to “No Punctuation" now across major music streaming platforms. beabadoobee's Bananas 4 Cats album will release on February 19, 2027.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast

Conversely, George Russell’s racing suit is finished in a striking blue hue, serving as a direct nod to the signature bluish glow Ceralume emits once darkness falls.Blending their material innovation with high-octane motorsport apparel, the contrasting suits turn the Mercedes-AMG PETRONAS duo into a striking visual spectacle of light and dark under the neon glow of the Las Vegas skyline. Entertainment.title: côte&ciel and Joe Chia’s “What We Carry” Collab Folds Cotton Into Fluid, Shape-Shifting Bags
Entertainment.text: Summarycôte&ciel and Joe Chia launch the "What We Carry" capsule collection.Origami-folded cotton LINGGI convertible backpack and fluid ENDAU crossbody bag.Available globally today with prices ranging from $310 - $370 USD.côte&ciel has teamed up with Malaysian minimalist designer Joe Chia on “What We Carry,” a two-piece bag capsule about how material and movement interact. Known for translating architectural geometry into ergonomic bags, côte&ciel meets Chia’s fluid, garment-focused tailoring in a project exploring both physical materiality and emotional weight.As Joe Goodwin from côte&ciel's marketing team notes, the duo aimed to unpack "what we carry" - not just literally, but emotionally - acknowledging how past experiences shape the way individuals move through the world. By filtering the brand's sculptural archives through Chia’s apparel sensibilities, the partnership creates what Goodwin describes as a sense of "jamais vu": an aesthetic that feels simultaneously familiar and entirely unexpected.Both bags are named after rivers in Malaysia, a nod to Joe Chia’s roots and the idea of flow. The LINGGI is a convertible backpack that also wears as a shoulder bag. Its crossed straps meet a soft, teardrop-shaped body that sags and fills out depending on its contents.As for the ENDAU, it's a crossbody that can also go over one shoulder. A single strap tapers into a sculpted, drop-like body, and in the product shots it hangs almost like draped fabric. Both bags are made from black cotton with a crinkled, textured surface. They’re built with an origami-style folded construction and have expandable main compartments that fit laptops up to 16 inches, though neither has a dedicated laptop sleeve.Small details tie the collaboration together. Satin-finish metal teardrop zip pulls carry embossed côte&ciel branding, and a black strap slider bears both brands’ names. Inside, a lined interior includes a zippered pocket for smaller items. The all-black, texture-led palette keeps the attention on shape and drape. The côte&ciel x Joe Chia “What We Carry” capsule launches globally today via coteetciel.com, with prices from $310 - $370 USD.Click here to view full gallery at Hypebeast
